title: Navigation for an independent hotel
metaTitle: Navigation for an independent hotel site
excerpt: Navigation should map guest jobs, not hotel departments. Use words travelers already say, and keep one header path that checks dates.
alt: A laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, beside a plant and a yellow mug, the quiet tools behind a menu a guest never sees.
caption: The menu a guest uses should be simpler than the tools that build it. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What labels belong in a hotel menu?
faqs.answer: Labels for the jobs guests arrive with: rooms, dates, rates, arrival, and a question the checker cannot answer. Use the room names regulars already say. Journal, experiences, and department names force a guess.

faqs.question: Where should check dates sit?
faqs.answer: In the header, in those words, on every page including the homepage. The link should open a checker, not a film or a contact form. Repeat the same verb at the end of long pages.

faqs.question: How deep should the menu be?
faqs.answer: One level is enough for a small house. If a second level exists, the parent item should be a real page, because phones and keyboards do not rely on hover. Keep news posts out of the header. Five to seven labels is a full menu.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Independent hotel website navigation should be a map of the jobs a traveler arrives with, not a map of your departments. For someone comparing three stays, the labels should be words they already use, and one path in the header should check dates. If a label only makes sense to the team, it is in the wrong menu.

WCAG groups its requirements under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A menu is an operable and understandable object. People have to find it, use it without guessing, and predict where a label will land. A beautiful menu that fails those tests is still a failed menu, including on a phone, which WCAG explicitly covers.

## The jobs they arrive with

Most travelers land with one of five jobs. See the room. Check whether specific dates are free. Understand what the rate includes. Work out how to arrive. Ask a question the checker cannot answer. Your navigation should be able to complete those jobs in a label or two. If it cannot, the page structure is wrong, and the menu is only the symptom.

Write the jobs down before you write the labels. A short list on paper is enough. Then point each job at a real URL. Room. Dates. Rates. Arrival. A question. If two jobs share a page, the label should name the job they will recognize, and the page should actually contain both. Do not point "Rates" at a homepage that hopes they will scroll.

Some guests arrive from a map listing with a narrower job: confirm you are the place they think you are, and find the door. "Find us" earns a label when the entrance is easy to miss. It does not earn a label when the page is only an embedded map with no sentence about the stair or the bell.

Ignore jobs that are really your jobs. Updating Instagram. Explaining the rebrand. Recruiting a cook. Those can be footer links if they must exist. They are not the menu a Friday-night guest needs.

## Labels they already use

Use Rooms, Dates, Rates, Breakfast, Arrival, and the name of the house. Use the room names your regulars say. If you have a dog policy that decides bookings, "Dogs" is a clearer label than "Policies," because the person with a dog is not browsing a policy center. They are answering one question.

Reject labels that sound like a magazine. Journal. Stories. Experiences. World. Sanctuary. A traveler comparing three stays will not open "World" to find a rate. They will assume the site is performing, and they will go back to a tab whose menu says "Rooms."

Reject internal words. F&B. Guest relations. Brand. The house. If "the house" is what you call the building and guests do not, it is a private nickname. You can use it in a sentence on the about page, once you have earned the context. You should not use it as a top-level label on a first visit.

Google's guidance on title links asks for descriptive titles that distinguish pages, not vague names and not the same boilerplate on every URL. The same standard belongs on the menu. The visible label and the page's heading should describe the same destination. "Stay" in the menu and "Our philosophy" on the page is a broken promise, even if both feel on-brand to the team.

Keep labels short enough to scan, and specific enough to choose. Two words is often right. A sentence in the menu is a paragraph that escaped. If you need a sentence, the page failed to earn a clear name, and the page should be rewritten before the menu grows a subtitle.

## One path that checks dates

The date check is the action of the site. It gets a stable place: a text label in the header that says "Check dates," visible on the first screen, on every page, including this one. Do not hide it inside "Book" if "Book" opens a mood page. Do not hide it under a hamburger on a wide screen where there was room for the word.

The path should open the checker, not a contact form and not a gallery. If your booking lives on another domain, the label should still say what will happen. "Check dates" that throws someone into a confusing engine with the dates stripped out is a path that looks right and works wrong. Carry the context you can carry. At minimum, land them where a search can start without a lecture.

Repeat the path at the end of long pages, in the same words. Header and closing link should match. A page that says "Check dates" at the top and "Begin your journey" at the bottom has two products. Keep one verb.

Do not add a second primary path that competes. "Gift vouchers" and "Join the club" can exist. They do not sit in the same visual weight as dates, or the menu has two missions and the guest has one. Weight is a design choice with a job attached: the eye should hit dates without hunting.

## What department names do

Department names comfort the org chart. Front of house. Marketing. Events. They are meaningful in a staff meeting. On the site they force a guest to guess which department holds the breakfast hours. Guessing is a tax, and the other hotel is not charging it.

If you run events that are a real business, give them a label the buyer uses. "Private hire" or "The whole house," with the boundary in the page, beats "Events," which might mean a public jazz night or a wedding. The label should match the contract you actually offer.

A restaurant you operate for people who are not staying is a separate job and deserves its own label, with a clear split between guest breakfast and public dinner. If you do not serve public dinner, do not leave a "Dining" label up because the template had one. Dead labels teach people that the menu is fiction.

Staff pages organized by department belong on the intranet. The guest-facing about page can name people by what they do at the desk, which is a job label, not a department label. Navigation and the about page should use the same nouns, or the site feels like two companies.

## How deep the menu should be

One level is the goal for a house with a handful of rooms. Rooms can open a short list if the room names matter and each room has a page worth opening. Dates should not have children. Rates should not have a submenu of seasons if the pricing page already shows the shape. Depth is where guests get lost and where you will forget to update a link.

If you need a second level, make the parent a real page too, not a dead hover. Some people never see hover menus. Some are using a keyboard or a phone. WCAG's operable principle is the practical rule: the destination has to be reachable without a lucky gesture. A tap should land somewhere useful, and the same links should be available without a mouse.

Dropdowns full of every blog post are a junk drawer. If you publish notes, one label, "Notes" or "From the house," can point at the list. Individual essays do not belong in the header. They change, and the header should be stable enough that a returning guest still knows where dates are.

Limit the header to the jobs. Five to seven labels, including dates. When you want an eighth, remove one. Menus grow by affection for new pages. They shrink by remembering the traveler's Friday night.

## Footer, header, and the page you are on

The header is for jobs. The footer is for the long tail: cancellation, privacy, a phone number, the company name, a way to the contact path. Do not invert this because the footer is where the template put the pretty links. A guest who needs the rate will not go hunting in the legal row on purpose. Some will, and they will be tired when they arrive.

Mark the current page. A menu that does not show where you are forces people to re-derive their place from the heading alone. On a small site that sounds minor. In a comparison, with three hotels open, it is how someone checks the wrong rate and thinks you changed the price.

The logo can go home. Home should then offer the room and the dates, or the logo is a loop. Do not make the logo the only way to check dates. A path that depends on a ritual is not a path. It is a puzzle.

External booking links should look external if they leave your site, in the sense that the guest is not surprised. The label does the work. You do not need a warning essay. You need the word "dates" to remain true on the other side.

## After they can find the room

Once the labels point at real jobs, the pages have to carry the room in pictures, or the menu is a promise with nothing behind it. Photography is the next decision, and it is easy to get wrong in a handsome way. [Which photographs belong on the site, and which pool film does not](/blog/photography-direction-for-an-independent-hotel) is the piece to read next. The menu can say "Rooms." The picture still has to be the room.

To see how a site can make those jobs obvious in the work itself, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Navigation is not a layer you add at the end. It is the list of jobs you were willing to support with a real page.
